unit.title: Teaching embedded and IoT systems at university

video.title: Real-time and the power budget: Deadlines and duty cycles
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Amina Bello - lecturer in education, Lagos
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: A student team promised a field sensor would run for a year on two AA cells. It died after nine days. The radio was never switched off.
Today: how to budget energy with duty cycles, what real-time really means, and how to schedule tasks so deadlines are met.
Battery life is capacity divided by average current. A device that sleeps most of the time has an average set by how long and how often it wakes. That fraction is the duty cycle.
Awake at twenty milliamps for one second in sixty, and asleep at ten microamps otherwise, the average is about a third of a milliamp. Two thousand milliamp hours then last roughly eight months.
In a typical LoRa sensor node, the radio uses most of the energy, even though it is on for a tiny fraction of the time. Sensing and the processor use far less.
Real-time does not mean fast. It means every task finishes before its deadline. A hard real-time miss is a failure, like an airbag. A soft miss only lowers quality, like a dropped video frame.

Give the shortest period the highest priority. Liu and Layland proved that n periodic tasks always meet their deadlines this way if total utilisation is below n times two to the one over n, minus one. For many tasks that tends to about sixty nine percent.
Quick check! A node draws fifty milliamps for one second every hundred seconds and almost nothing otherwise. What is its average current?
Half a milliamp: fifty times one in a hundred. So halving the wake time doubles battery life far more cheaply than a bigger battery.
In the app, open the battery lab. Change how often it reports, the radio and the battery, and watch the predicted battery life.

Your turn. Two tasks: one needs one millisecond every four, the other needs two milliseconds every ten. Is the total utilisation under the rate-monotonic bound for two tasks, about eighty three percent?
Yes: a quarter plus a fifth is forty five percent. Remember: battery life follows average current, the radio dominates, and real-time means meeting deadlines.

scenes.on_screen_text: Try it in your next lab
scenes.narration: Try it in your next lab: give each team a current meter and their own sensor node. They measure active and sleep current, then predict battery life and defend the number.

checkpoints.prompt: A node draws 50 mA for 1 s every 100 s and almost nothing otherwise. Average current?
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: average = duty cycle × active current = 1/100 × 50 = 0.5 mA.
